**Aida**
Verdi's 1871 opera set in ancient Egypt, which premiered in Cairo. The Egyptian commander Radamès loves Aida, an enslaved Ethiopian princess whose father, King Amonasro, is at war with Egypt. The Egyptian princess Amneris is her rival. Radamès receives the sacred arms at the Temple of Vulcan, and the opera features a grand "Triumphal March." At the end, Radamès is condemned as a traitor and entombed beneath the temple, where Aida joins him to die.

**La traviata**
Verdi's 1853 opera based on Alexandre Dumas fils's The Lady of the Camellias. The courtesan Violetta Valéry falls in love with Alfredo Germont. Alfredo's father, Giorgio Germont, persuades her to leave him, and she pretends to love Baron Douphol. At a gambling party, Alfredo throws his winnings at her feet, and in the last act Violetta dies of tuberculosis in his arms.

**Rigoletto**
Verdi's 1851 opera about the hunchbacked court jester of the womanizing Duke of Mantua. A courtier's curse falls on Rigoletto, who hires the assassin Sparafucile to kill the Duke. Instead, his daughter Gilda sacrifices herself, and Rigoletto finds her body in a sack and cries "La maledizione!" ("The curse!").

**"La donna è mobile"**
The Duke of Mantua's famous aria in Rigoletto, whose title means "woman is fickle." When Rigoletto hears the Duke singing it in the distance, he realizes the body in the sack is not the Duke's.

**"Va, pensiero" (Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves)**
The chorus from Nabucco (1842), Verdi's first major success, in which the exiled Hebrews in Babylon long for their homeland, asking their thoughts to fly "on golden wings." Nabucco is about the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, who later prays to the Hebrew God. The chorus became an anthem of Italian nationalism.

**Il trovatore and the "Anvil Chorus"**
Il trovatore ("The Troubadour," 1853) is set in 15th-century Spain, where the Count di Luna pursues the troubadour Manrico, his rival for Leonora. In the "Anvil Chorus," Roma workers strike anvils at dawn. The Roma woman Azucena sings "Stride la vampa" about her mother being burned at the stake. Leonora takes poison from her ring rather than give herself to di Luna, and Manrico turns out to be di Luna's own brother.

**"Libiamo ne' lieti calici"**
The drinking song (brindisi) sung by Alfredo and Violetta at the party in Act I of La traviata. The same act ends with Violetta's showpiece aria "Sempre libera," during which Alfredo's voice is heard singing of love in the distance. In the last act, the reunited lovers sing "Gran Dio! Morir sì giovine" ("Great God! To die so young").

**Un ballo in maschera (A Masked Ball)**
An opera about the assassination of King Gustav III of Sweden at a masked ball. Censors forced Verdi to move the setting to colonial Boston, where the king becomes Governor Riccardo. The fortune-teller Ulrica predicts that Riccardo will be killed by the next man who shakes his hand, who turns out to be his friend Renato.

**La forza del destino (The Force of Destiny)**
An opera based on the Spanish play Don Álvaro, o la fuerza del sino. Leonora, daughter of the Marquis of Calatrava, loves Don Álvaro, who accidentally kills her father when his thrown pistol goes off. Its overture opens with three unison E's in the brass.

**Otello**
Verdi's late opera based on Shakespeare's Othello, with a libretto by Arrigo Boito. It opens in a storm with Otello's entrance aria "Esultate!", in which he celebrates the defeat of "the Muslim's pride." In Act IV, Desdemona sings the "Willow Song," repeating "Salce," before her "Ave Maria."

**Requiem**
Verdi's Messa da Requiem (1874), written in memory of the novelist Alessandro Manzoni. Its Dies irae alternates loud G minor orchestral chords with offbeat bass drum strokes, and its Tuba mirum features trumpet fanfares, including offstage trumpets.

**Don Carlos**
A grand opera based on Friedrich Schiller's play about Don Carlos, the son of King Philip II of Spain. It ends with a figure who seems to be the ghost of Carlos's grandfather, Emperor Charles V, pulling Carlos into the cloister of a monastery.

**"Caro nome"**
Gilda's aria in Rigoletto, in which she dreams of her disguised lover, actually the Duke. It is accompanied by two flutes and is a coloratura showpiece for the soprano.

**"Ritorna vincitor!"**
Aida's aria ("Return victorious!"), in which she is torn between her love for Radamès, who is leading Egypt's army, and her loyalty to her father and her Ethiopian homeland.
